input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-455: Principles of Cybersecurity. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: This course provides a broad introduction to cybersecurity principles and practices, and emphasizes policies and mechanisms for building secure and trusted computer systems. It will cover cybersecurity principles, policies and mechanisms; core knowledge areas of data, software, component, connection, system, human, organizational and societal security; and crosscutting concepts of confidentiality, integrity, availability, risk, adversarial thinking, and systems thinking. Topics in privacy, and legal and ethical aspects will also be emphasized. Presentations, reports and projects are required. Students cannot take and receive credit for this course if they have credit for CSCI-655. This course requires the knowledge of computer science theory and concepts of computer systems. Prerequisites: CSCI-250 and (CSCI-262 or CSCI-263) or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Spring

Source excerpts:

[nist-cryptographic-standards]
Cryptographic standards define approved algorithms and parameters. Encryption supports confidentiality when keys and modes are used correctly. Message authentication and digital signatures address integrity and authenticity in different ways. Random number generation supports keys, nonces, and other security parameters. Key management covers generation, distribution, storage, use, rotation, revocation, and destruction. Modes of operation define how a primitive processes data larger than one block. Validation checks implementations against specified requirements. Security depends on the complete protocol and implementation, not only an algorithm name. Analysis also considers side channels and migration requirements.

[nist-ssdf]
The Secure Software Development Framework groups practices into four practice groups. Prepare the Organization establishes people, processes, and technology for secure development. Protect the Software prevents unauthorized access to code and development artifacts. Produce Well-Secured Software addresses security requirements, design, verification, and release. Respond to Vulnerabilities identifies, analyzes, remediates, and learns from discovered weaknesses. Security requirements should be tracked throughout development. Verification provides evidence that selected practices and controls were performed. Security reasoning identifies assets, trust boundaries, threats, controls, evidence, residual risk, and responsibilities.

[rit-csci-455]
This course provides a broad introduction to cybersecurity principles and practices, and emphasizes policies and mechanisms for building secure and trusted computer systems. It will cover cybersecurity principles, policies and mechanisms; core knowledge areas of data, software, component, connection, system, human, organizational and societal security; and crosscutting concepts of confidentiality, integrity, availability, risk, adversarial thinking, and systems thinking. Topics in privacy, and legal and ethical aspects will also be emphasized. Presentations, reports and projects are required. Students cannot take and receive credit for this course if they have credit for CSCI-655. This course requires the knowledge of computer science theory and concepts of computer systems. Prerequisites: CSCI-250 and (CSCI-262 or CSCI-263) or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Spring

beats.claim: Confidentiality, integrity, and availability form the core triad of security properties that protect information and systems.
beats.example: A hospital's electronic health records must remain confidential from unauthorized users, maintain integrity against tampering, and remain available during peak patient intake hours.
beats.title: Lesson Title: Foundations of Cybersecurity Principles
beats.visualDirection: Display a simple Venn diagram showing the overlapping circles of confidentiality, integrity, and availability, with a central 'Secure System' label.

beats.claim: Cryptographic standards define approved algorithms and parameters that enable encryption to support confidentiality when keys and modes are used correctly.
beats.example: AES-256 encryption with proper key management ensures patient data remains unreadable to unauthorized personnel, satisfying confidentiality requirements.
beats.title: Lesson Title: Cryptographic Standards and Confidentiality
beats.visualDirection: Show a flowchart: Plaintext -> Encryption Algorithm (AES-256) -> Ciphertext, with a lock icon labeled 'Confidentiality'.

beats.claim: Message authentication and digital signatures address integrity and authenticity in different ways, ensuring data has not been altered.
beats.example: A digital signature on a software update verifies the developer's identity and confirms the code has not been modified during transmission.
beats.title: Lesson Title: Integrity and Authentication Mechanisms
beats.visualDirection: Display a side-by-side comparison: Hash-based message authentication (integrity check) vs. Digital signature (integrity + authenticity).

beats.claim: The Secure Software Development Framework groups practices into four practice groups: Prepare the Organization, Protect the Software, Produce Well-Secured Software, and Respond to
beats.example: A development team uses the 'Prepare the Organization' group to establish secure coding standards and training before writing any code.
beats.title: Lesson Title: Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF)
beats.visualDirection: Create a four-step circular diagram labeled with the four SSDF practice groups, connected by arrows indicating iterative flow.

beats.claim: Security requirements should be tracked throughout development, and verification provides evidence that selected practices and controls were performed.
beats.example: A compliance officer reviews a checklist to verify that all encryption standards and access controls were implemented before software release.
beats.title: Lesson Title: Security Requirements and Verification
beats.visualDirection: Show a checklist graphic with checkboxes next to security requirements, highlighting 'Verification' as the final step.

beats.claim: Respond to Vulnerabilities identifies, analyzes, remediates, and learns from discovered weaknesses, closing the security lifecycle.
beats.example: After a penetration test reveals an unpatched database vulnerability, the team patches the code, updates documentation, and trains developers on secure input validation.
beats.title: Lesson Title: Vulnerability Management and Response
beats.visualDirection: Display a feedback loop diagram: Vulnerability Discovery -> Analysis -> Remediation -> Learning/Improvement.

beats.claim: Security reasoning identifies assets, trust boundaries, threats, controls, evidence, residual risk, and responsibilities to guide defensive design.
beats.example: An analyst maps a web application's trust boundary, identifies a potential SQL injection threat, and assigns a control to validate all user inputs.
beats.title: Lesson Title: Adversarial Thinking and Threat Modeling
beats.visualDirection: Show a trust boundary diagram with internal assets, external threats, and a labeled 'Control' zone between them.

beats.claim: Systems thinking evaluates how confidentiality, integrity, availability, risk, and policy mechanisms interact across data, software, and human components.
beats.example: A policy requiring multi-factor authentication reduces risk by addressing both human behavior and system access points simultaneously.
beats.title: Lesson Title: Systems Thinking and Crosscutting Concepts
beats.visualDirection: Create a layered system model showing data, software, human, and policy layers, with arrows indicating cross-cutting security concepts.

beats.claim: Privacy, legal, and ethical aspects must be integrated into security policies to ensure responsible and compliant system design.
beats.example: A healthcare app implements data minimization and consent mechanisms to comply with privacy regulations while maintaining security.
beats.title: Lesson Title: Privacy, Ethics, and Legal Compliance
beats.visualDirection: Display a balance scale graphic with 'Security' on one side and 'Privacy/Ethics/Legal' on the other, labeled 'Balanced Design'.

beats.claim: Students must apply foundational concepts to evaluate real-world scenarios using a structured checklist for confidentiality, integrity, availability, and risk.
beats.example: An auditor reviews a cloud migration plan against the checklist to verify encryption, access controls, backup availability, and risk mitigation steps.
beats.title: Lesson Title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Show a printable checklist template with columns for 'Component', 'Confidentiality', 'Integrity', 'Availability', 'Risk Level', and 'Mitigation'.

learningObjectives: Define the core crosscutting concepts of confidentiality, integrity, and availability as foundational security properties.
Explain how the Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) practice groups structure secure software development processes.
Apply adversarial thinking and systems thinking to analyze real-world security risks and policy mechanisms.
